knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

```{r setup}
library(panelcointr)
```

## The tests

Westerlund (2007) tests the null hypothesis of no cointegration by asking
whether the error-correction term of a conditional error-correction model
is zero. For each unit $i$,

$$
\Delta y_{it} = \delta_i' d_t + \alpha_i y_{i,t-1} + \lambda_i' x_{i,t-1}
  + \sum_{j=1}^{p_i} \alpha_{ij} \Delta y_{i,t-j}
  + \sum_{j=-q_i}^{p_i} \gamma_{ij}' \Delta x_{i,t-j} + e_{it},
$$

and the null is $\alpha_i = 0$ for all $i$. Unlike residual-based tests,
this does not impose a common-factor restriction, which can cost them a
lot of power.

There are four statistics. The group-mean statistics $G_\tau$ (`Gt`) and
$G_\alpha$ (`Ga`) average unit-level t-ratios and coefficients and test
against $\alpha_i < 0$ for at least one unit. The panel statistics
$P_\tau$ (`Pt`) and $P_\alpha$ (`Pa`) pool the information on a common
$\alpha$ and test against $\alpha_i = \alpha < 0$ for all units. All four
are left-tailed. Asymptotic p-values come from the moments of the paper's
Table 1; bootstrap p-values are robust to cross-sectional dependence.

## Health care expenditure and GDP

The `hce` data are the paper's application: per-capita health care
expenditure and GDP for 20 OECD countries, 1970 to 2001.

```{r}
str(hce)
```

Both series trend, so the model has a constant and a trend. With lags and
leads chosen by AIC between 1 and 3 and between 0 and 3, and the default
bandwidth $\lfloor 4 (T/100)^{2/9} \rfloor = 3$:

```{r}
fit <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                         deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3))
fit
```

All four tests reject the null of no cointegration at the 5% level with
the asymptotic p-values.

## Reproducing Stata's xtwest

The defaults follow the paper. The Stata command `xtwest` (Persyn and
Westerlund 2008) departs from it in several places, for example by
normalising $G_\alpha$ with the residual degrees of freedom, using the
average lag length for the panel statistics, and comparing information
criteria across samples of different sizes. `compat = "xtwest"` reproduces
it, and `compat = "xtwest_westerlund"` reproduces its `westerlund` option.
The three calls of Persyn and Westerlund (2008) give their published
output:

```{r}
runs <- list(
  list(lags = 1, leads = 1, lrwindow = 3, compat = "xtwest"),
  list(lags = c(1, 2), leads = c(0, 1), lrwindow = 2, compat = "xtwest"),
  list(lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3), lrwindow = 3, compat = "xtwest_westerlund")
)
published <- rbind(c(-2.681, -10.927, -12.035, -10.524),
                   c(-2.736, -11.254, -12.859, -11.773),
                   c(-4.082, -27.702, -12.969, -22.470))
ours <- t(sapply(runs, function(a) {
  r <- do.call(pcoint_westerlund,
               c(list(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                      deterministic = "trend"), a))
  r$statistics$value
}))
colnames(published) <- colnames(ours) <- c("Gt", "Ga", "Pt", "Pa")
knitr::kable(cbind(run = 1:3, round(ours, 3)), caption = "panelcointr")
knitr::kable(cbind(run = 1:3, published), caption = "Published xtwest output")
```

The only difference is in the last digit of Ga in the second call. The
value is -11.2535, which `xtwest` prints as -11.254 because Stata stores
its intermediate variables in single precision.

The third call also matches the z-values of the paper's Table 7
(-9.613, -10.626, -4.100, -10.119), which were computed with the moments
hard-coded in `xtwest`'s `westerlund` option:

```{r}
r3 <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                        deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3),
                        lrwindow = 3, compat = "xtwest_westerlund")
round(r3$statistics$z, 3)
```

`?westerlund_control` lists every difference and lets you switch each one
on its own. For example, `xtwest` compares the information criterion of
each lag order on that order's own sample. The choice then depends on the
units of `y`: multiplying `loghex` by 3 changes `xtwest`'s selected
orders, while the default comparison on a common sample does not.

```{r}
hce3 <- transform(hce, loghex = 3 * loghex)
avg_orders <- function(data, ...) {
  r <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = data, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                         deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 2), leads = c(0, 1),
                         lrwindow = 2, ...)
  c(lags = mean(r$units$lags), leads = mean(r$units$leads))
}
rbind(xtwest = avg_orders(hce, compat = "xtwest"),
      xtwest_rescaled = avg_orders(hce3, compat = "xtwest"),
      default = avg_orders(hce),
      default_rescaled = avg_orders(hce3))
```

## Bootstrap p-values

The asymptotic p-values assume that the units are cross-sectionally
independent, which is doubtful for OECD aggregates. The bootstrap of the
paper's Section 5 resamples whole periods (the same periods for all
units) from the null-imposed residuals, which preserves any
cross-sectional dependence. The indices are drawn with R's random number
generator, so `set.seed()` makes the results reproducible whatever the
number of threads.

```{r}
set.seed(2007)
fit_boot <- pcoint_westerlund(loghex ~ loggdp, data = hce, index = c("ctr", "year"),
                              deterministic = "trend", lags = c(1, 3), leads = c(0, 3),
                              bootstrap = 499, n_threads = 2)
fit_boot
```

The bootstrap p-values are much larger than the asymptotic ones. With
$T = 32$, up to three lags and leads chosen by AIC, and cross-sectionally
dependent data, the null distributions are far to the left of their
asymptotic counterparts (compare the bootstrap critical values in
`summary()` below), and the evidence of cointegration is much weaker. The
paper's Table 7 reports bootstrap rejections. Those use Westerlund's
original settings, which `compat = "xtwest_westerlund"` reproduces, and
the original bootstrap code, which differs from the one here in its
initialisation, centring and lag selection. Its bootstrap p-values cannot
be reproduced exactly. `plot()` shows the bootstrap distributions:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit_boot)
```

## Unit-level results

`summary()` adds the bootstrap critical values, the distribution of the
selected orders, the mean-group error-correction model and the unit-level
results:

```{r}
summary(fit_boot)
```

The `units` element holds the unit-level estimates, and `coefficients`
holds each unit's full error-correction model:

```{r}
head(fit$units)
```

## References

Persyn, D. and Westerlund, J. (2008). Error-correction-based cointegration
tests for panel data. *Stata Journal* 8(2), 232-241.

Westerlund, J. (2007). Testing for error correction in panel data.
*Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics* 69(6), 709-748.
